Reference profile

How to run CALIBER as the reference deployment: the one shape that refuses to start on an unsafe setting, every requirement with its variable and reason, and a configuration that passes.

OperatorReferenceBETA
PrerequisitesA PostgreSQL database and a way to set environment variables for the CALIBER process
Reviewed 2026-10-26 · current main branch docs contract

Use this page to run CALIBER as the reference deployment: one supported shape that refuses to start while any of the settings below is unsafe. It is the deployment the EGI reference architecture's claims (governed action, safe restart, evidence) are made about; docs/architecture/adr/0001-reference-profile.md defines the whole shape, and this page lists what the process itself enforces today.

Turn it on#

Set CALIBER_PROFILE=reference. The default, development, starts with whatever is configured and behaves exactly as before. Under reference, create_app checks the configuration before it opens the database or creates the bootstrap account, so a refused start leaves nothing behind, and it lists every violation at once:

reference profile refused (2 violations):
- database_url is a SQLite file; set CALIBER_DATABASE_URL=<a PostgreSQL URL> for the reference profile
- csrf_enabled is false; set CALIBER_CSRF_ENABLED=true for the reference profile

An unknown profile name is a configuration error. GET /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/readiness carries a profile field, so an operator can see which rules the running process was started under.

What it requires#

violation codesettingenvironment variablerequiredwhy

The messages in the refusal name the setting and the variable to change. The table is checked by caliber/tests/test_profile.py: a rule that is not listed here, or a row without a rule, fails the build.

What it also does at runtime#

Beyond refusing to start, the reference profile bounds every request body: a body above CALIBER_REFERENCE_MAX_BODY_BYTES (default 1 MiB) is answered 413 with {"reason": "request_too_large", "max_bytes": N}, whether the client declared a large Content-Length or streamed the body without one (or understated it). The check is the outermost layer, so an oversized request is refused before authentication, CSRF or routing reads it. A request at exactly the limit is accepted, and the development profile installs no limit.

Two kinds of request have a limit of their own, because their routes accept more than 1 MiB. The larger limit applies; the default is never lower than a route's own:

requestlimitsetting
multipart/form-data (skill zips, attachments, workspace imports, storage objects)256 MiBCALIBER_REFERENCE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES; raise it together with CALIBER_WORKFLOW_STORAGE_MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES (250 MiB), which each route still enforces, tighter, afterwards
the GitHub webhook routeCALIBER_GITHUB_WEBHOOK_MAX_BODY_BYTES (2 MiB)the route's own setting; the global 1 MiB never lowers it

A refusal carries x-request-id (the caller's, or one generated) and writes one warning log line naming the method, path and size. The body is refused, not drained, so a client that keeps sending a very large body may see a connection reset rather than the 413.

Memory is owned, derived and read-mostly#

Until the owned memory lifecycle (M20: retention, legal hold, deletion) exists, the reference profile does not offer free-form durable memory (B12 memory, #667). The /memory API and the in-run memory tools behave as follows:

  • No free-form partition. agent_id must name an agent or workflow, and run_id a workflow run, that the caller can see; user_id must be the caller's own identity, admins included. A scope value that is present but not a non-empty string is a 400, not ignored. A run id alone is refused (403).
  • The partition is pinned to the caller. With an agent_id, the memory is the caller's own within that agent or workflow (the server adds user_id); with none, it is the caller's own namespace, qualified by the active project (<project>:<user>). A client never chooses whose memory a read or write reaches, and metadata may not carry user_id, agent_id, run_id or actor_id (400), because mem0 filters on those stored fields.
  • One refusal, no disclosure. A partition that does not exist, one that belongs to another project or user, and a label that names nothing all answer 404 memory partition not found; no id is echoed.
  • Writes are verbatim. POST /memory requires infer=false (403 otherwise), because LLM-inferred writes create durable facts nobody owns; and startup refuses CALIBER_MEMORY_INFER=true while memory is enabled (table above).
  • No bulk deletion. DELETE /memory answers 403: deleting memory needs the lifecycle's retention and legal-hold rules.
  • Bounded reads. top_k is capped at 100.
  • In-run tools. memory_search, memory_add, memory_list and list_entities act on the run initiator's memory within the workflow (the initiator is set by the server, never by the model); a run with no initiator gets no memory tools.
  • Same rules below the route. The service layer refuses bulk delete, inferred writes, run-only partitions and partition keys in metadata (MemoryLifecycleUnavailableError). It does not itself check that an agent_id or user_id belongs to the caller: the route and the in-run tool binding do that and are the only callers.

The development profile keeps the previous behaviour. Known limitation: the installed mem0 2.x rejects entity ids passed as top-level search/list arguments, which the service does today (also in development); until that is fixed (tracked separately) search and list through the memory service return an error.

A configuration that passes#

CALIBER_PROFILE=reference
CALIBER_DATABASE_URL=postgresql+psycopg://caliber:CHANGE_ME@db.internal:5432/caliber
CALIBER_AUTH_MODE=session
CALIBER_AUTH_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD_ENV=CALIBER_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD
CALIBER_AUTH_BOOTSTRAP_ALLOW_INSECURE_DEFAULT=false
CALIBER_AUTH_DEV_FALLBACK_ENABLED=false
CALIBER_ADMIN_USERS=admin
CALIBER_APPROVER_USERS=approver
CALIBER_CSRF_ENABLED=true
CALIBER_CSRF_SIGNING_SECRET_ENV=CALIBER_CSRF_SIGNING_SECRET
CALIBER_EGRESS_POLICY_ENABLED=true
CALIBER_MCP_ALLOW_INSECURE_HTTP=false
CALIBER_APPROVAL_ALLOW_SELF_APPROVAL=false

Two of the variables name other variables that hold secrets (CALIBER_BOOTSTRAP_PASSWORD and CALIBER_CSRF_SIGNING_SECRET); set those in your secret store, not in this file. What happens when they are missing differs, and neither case is a profile refusal:

  • No CSRF signing secret: with CSRF on, the server refuses to boot (a RuntimeError, not the profile's ConfigError). That check runs after the database is opened and the bootstrap account is written, so unlike a profile refusal it can leave those behind.
  • No bootstrap password: the server starts and logs a warning, but nobody can sign in.
  • No role lists: CALIBER_ADMIN_USERS, CALIBER_OPERATOR_USERS and CALIBER_APPROVER_USERS default to empty, and the bootstrap account is then a viewer that cannot create projects; the server logs an error. The example names an admin and an approver. Because self-approval is refused, an approver must be a different account from whoever starts a run.

The database must be migrated (caliber-migrate) before the first start.

A stored secret never leaves the platform#

caliber/tests/test_secret_canary.py (B12.5b, #666) stores EGI_CANARY_<uuid4> as egi-canary through the encrypted secret store, points llm_api_key_env at secret://egi-canary, and runs the core journey over HTTP with logging at DEBUG: sign in (the trusted proxy header), create a project, register an agent, publish, promote and run a workflow, run a calibration run to a candidate and apply it, read the LLM provider status (which resolves the secret inside the request; the test fails if nothing in the journey did), and export the audit log, plus refused requests. It fails if the value appears in any response (status, headers, cookies, body; the helper calls too), any log record (message, arguments, extra fields as the JSON formatter renders them, traceback), any caliber_workflow_run_events row or any audit row. The failure paths of resolution (a revoked secret, corrupted ciphertext, a provider built from a revoked secret) are scanned the same way, and a control test plants the value in every scanned surface to prove the scan can fail. It runs in the Backend core job and the full backend suite.

Not covered: the prompt registry routes and MLflow traces need a live MLflow registry, which ordinary CI does not have; the journey's prompts are the agent prompts in the workflow manifest, which the calibration run rewrites. Sign-in by session login is covered by test_auth_sessions, not by this journey.

Running it found that CALIBER_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG with the default S3 log sink recursed: the S3 client's own DEBUG records re-entered the handler, so each record caused a growing number of S3 writes. The handler now ignores records emitted while it delivers a batch.

Run manifests are written once#

Migration 0114 adds caliber_run_manifests (B02.1a, #656): one row per workflow run holding the canonical manifest bytes (manifest_bytes) and their SHA-256 (manifest_digest). The row is immutable:

  • a database trigger refuses UPDATE and DELETE on SQLite and PostgreSQL (PostgreSQL also refuses TRUNCATE), so a bulk SQL statement fails as well as an ORM one: caliber_run_manifests is immutable: UPDATE refused;
  • the ORM raises ImmutableRecordError before any SQL for an instance update or delete and for an ORM update()/delete() statement (Session.bulk_*_mappings and Core/raw SQL skip the ORM and are refused by the trigger instead);
  • a second manifest for the same run violates uq_run_manifest_run, and a digest that is not the SHA-256 of the bytes is refused (by the ORM everywhere, and by a CHECK on PostgreSQL).

Runtime role. The migration revokes UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE on the table from PUBLIC. That only protects a deployment that runs the application as a role other than the table's owner, and caliber-migrate, scripts/install.sh and the shipped compose files use one database URL for both, so by default the application is the owner and is held only by the triggers and the ORM guard. For the privilege layer, run caliber-migrate as the owner and the application as a role granted only what it needs:

GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON caliber_run_manifests TO caliber_runtime;
GRANT SELECT ON caliber_workflow_runs TO caliber_runtime;  -- already held; the insert trigger reads it
-- no UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE on caliber_run_manifests; avoid ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES ... GRANT ALL

A trigger can be disabled by the table's owner or by a session with session_replication_role = replica; only the missing privilege holds against the runtime role. The reference profile does not check which role the application connects as (listed under "Not enforced yet"). The trigger functions are pinned to the migration's schema with pg_temp last in search_path, so a temporary table cannot shadow caliber_workflow_runs.

Legacy runs. caliber_workflow_runs.manifest_legacy is true by default, so every run that existed when 0114 ran, and every run created by a path other than admission, is legacy. Such a run has no manifest and can never get one (a manifest needs an existing, non-legacy run, also raised for a run that does not exist), and the flag cannot be changed afterwards (caliber_workflow_runs.manifest_legacy is write-once), so a historical pin cannot be fabricated. Admission (#680, below) creates a run with manifest_legacy = false in the same transaction as its manifest. A client with DELETE on runs can still delete a legacy run and re-insert the same id as a non-legacy one; that needs write access to runs and is not guarded here.

Retention and deletion. A run that has a manifest is retained evidence: retention pruning (CALIBER_WORKFLOW_RUN_RETENTION_DAYS) skips it, and DELETE /workflows/{id} answers 409 (cannot delete workflow: its runs have immutable run manifests) while any of its runs has one, because removing the run would either violate the manifest's foreign key (PostgreSQL) or orphan it (SQLite). Legacy and manifest-less runs are pruned and deleted as before. A rollback (caliber-migrate downgrade 0113) drops the table and therefore the manifests, never the runs; upgrading again starts with no manifests and marks every existing run legacy.

Reading a run's manifest (B02.5, #695)#

Two endpoints, two different manifests; neither changes the other.

endpointwhat it returns
GET /workflow-runs/{run_id}/manifest (unchanged)the workflow manifest the run executed: workflow_run_id, workflow_id, workflow_version_id, manifest_mode, manifest_hash, manifest. Served for every run, legacy included.
GET /workflow-runs/{run_id}/admission-manifest (new)the run's immutable admission manifest: workflow_run_id, schema_version, legacy, manifest_id, run_manifest (the stored record verbatim: pins, subject, workload, purpose, scope, grant id, request digest) and manifest_digest (the SHA-256 of its canonical bytes, so a reader can check it).

The new endpoint needs the same access as reading the run (a run you cannot see is 404, indistinguishable from a missing one) plus a role in the run's project (read): a caller who can see a run, for example through a public workflow, but has no role in its project also gets that same 404, never the project's name. A run with no project is gated by the workflow's visibility alone. A legacy run (admission was off, or a path that is not admitted) answers 200 with legacy: true and schema_version, manifest_id, run_manifest and manifest_digest all null: no history is fabricated. An admitted run whose stored manifest does not read back, is missing or is not in canonical form (so its digest could not be checked) is 409 (manifest_corrupt / manifest_missing). The SDK has client.workflows.runs.admission_manifest(run_id) (sync) and client.workflows.admission_manifest(run_id) (async), returning an AdmissionManifest (legacy is None, never "admitted", when the server did not say); the console API client has getWorkflowRunAdmissionManifest. run_manifest is the stored record verbatim, so it carries the subject's user id, the grant id, the request digest and, when a rule bundle is pinned, its absolute server path: treat the endpoint as project-member-visible evidence.

Building a manifest (admission, #676)#

caliber/src/caliber/run_manifest.py turns resolved inputs into the manifest record and its canonical bytes. It is a pure function: no SQL, clock, randomness or provider call, so the same input always gives the same bytes and digest. It does not choose or persist the manifest (admission, #680 and #684, does); the caller stores BuiltManifest.row_values() with CaliberRunManifest.

pinned = pin_rule_bundle(path, expected_sha256)          # only when rule bundles are enabled; reads the file once
built = build_run_manifest(
    manifest_id=new_manifest_id(), workflow_run_id=run_id, pins=ResolvedPins(...),
    subject=Subject(...), workload=Workload.for_workflow(name, digest), purpose="...",
    scope=DeploymentScope.fixed(project_id), created_at=now_utc,
    rule_bundle=pinned, rule_bundles_enabled=True,
)
  • Resolved, never named. Every pin must be the concrete value the run will use, and resolving it is the caller's duty: the builder cannot see the database, so it rejects what it can recognise as a moving target. After Unicode (NFKC) folding, a segment that is a floating word (latest, current, head, default, stable, main, master, nightly, ... as in v-latest or gpt-4o-latest), a wildcard version segment (1.x) or a range or wildcard character (*, ^, >=, ${...}) is unresolved_pin; a prompt, tool or skill pin is exactly <name>@<version> and only the version is checked; bundle_digest is a full lowercase SHA-256. Strings must be NFC, at most 512 characters (64 for the manifest and run ids), and lists at most 256 entries. Lists are sorted and may not repeat (duplicate_pin), so the order of resolution never changes the digest. A manifest is never filled in later.
  • Fixed scope. DeploymentScope carries organization (tenant_id), project, region and residency, all server-derived and enforced: the builder refuses (bad_scope) a scope whose organization, region or residency is not the deployment's (local in the reference profile, ADR 0001). A caller that names another organization is organization_switch; a subject acting in another project than the run's scope is project_mismatch. The manifest records project_id (optional in the v1 schema, absent for a run outside any project).
  • Rule bundle. When rule bundles are enabled the bundle is loaded and verified first (pin_rule_bundle, #726): a missing, oversized, changed or malformed file is rule_bundle_refused and no manifest is built; a verified bundle's absolute path and SHA-256 are recorded (make one PinnedRuleBundle per admission: it is a snapshot, not a handle on the file). Enabled without one is rule_bundle_required; one given while disabled is rule_bundle_unexpected. The digest in the manifest is the digest of the bytes that were verified, so editing the file afterwards changes nothing about this run (the context code re-verifies the bytes when it uses them, #736).
  • The request digest. request_digest (optional, 64 lowercase hex) is the SHA-256 of the canonical admission intent (see "Admitting a run"). A malformed one is bad_pin. It is part of the sealed bytes, so it cannot change after admission.
  • The digest excludes itself. manifest_digest is the SHA-256 of the canonical bytes (sorted keys, no whitespace, UTF-8, no NaN); the record carries no digest field.
  • Self-consistent result. BuiltManifest re-reads its own bytes on construction (digest, schema, UTF-8, no duplicate key or lone surrogate), so bytes and digest cannot disagree; row_values() includes created_at.
  • Strict writer, tolerant reader. The builder is stricter than the v1 schema (which takes any non-empty string), so records written before it still validate and read_manifest(bytes, digest) still reads them.
codemeaningrecovery
unresolved_pina pin is empty, missing or a floating selectorresolve it to a version or digest, then retry
bad_pina pin has the wrong type or shape (for example a digest that is not 64 lowercase hex)fix the resolver
duplicate_pinthe same reference twice (a knowledge base may be pinned at several versions, each once)name each once
bad_scopea scope field is empty or not a clean identifierfix the deployment configuration
organization_switchthe caller asked for another organizationnone: this deployment serves one organization
project_mismatchthe subject's project is not the run's projectadmit the run in the subject's project
bad_fieldmanifest id, run id, purpose or timestamp is malformed (a naive datetime)supply clean values and an aware time
rule_bundle_refusedthe configured bundle's bytes are missing, changed or invalidrestore the bundle or update the pinned digest deliberately
rule_bundle_required / rule_bundle_unexpectedenabled without a verified bundle / a bundle while disabledalign the configuration and the call
invalid_manifeststored bytes are not a valid manifest, or do not match their digest (read_manifest)treat as corruption: the row is immutable evidence

Admitting a run (B02.2a, #680)#

With admission on (always under CALIBER_PROFILE=reference, otherwise CALIBER_ADMISSION_ENABLED=true), every run a user queues is admitted: the run, its grant, its policy decision and its immutable manifest are created in one transaction, or none of them are. The paths covered are the create-run route (POST /workflow-runs), a retry of a failed run (POST /workflow-runs/{id}/retry, a new run admitted afresh), the event trigger (POST /workflows/{id}/trigger) and the assistant's run_workflow tool. The first three authenticate and check resource.execute in the workflow's project before admission; the assistant path checks the workflow's visibility first and the caller's role when the grant is issued (inside the same transaction, with the same outcome). A synchronous real run (POST /workflow-versions/{id}/run) is never queued, so with admission on it is refused (409, sync_run_not_admitted): use the queue.

  1. Pins first. Before any row is written, everything the run depends on is taken from the version's sealed deployment bundle (prompts, tools, MCP tools, skills, knowledge-base versions, the models its agents name, the policy version, the bundle's own digest) and the configured rule bundle is loaded and verified (CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_PATH/_SHA256). The manifest is built by the builder. A version that was never compiled, whose bundle fails its integrity check, or that has an unresolved runtime dependency, is refused (409, bundle_unavailable); so is a rule bundle that is missing or changed (manifest_refused: rule_bundle_refused). An unresolved evaluation dataset does not stop a run. The worker executes exactly what the pins describe: an admitted run's manifest snapshot is the bundle's sealed resolved manifest (prompts inline, tool versions exact, knowledge-base versions and child workflows resolved), not the authoring manifest, so moving a prompt alias after admission changes nothing about the run. (Skills are embedded in the bundle's snapshots; embedding and chat models of knowledge nodes are not part of the model pins yet.)
  2. One transaction. The run is inserted with manifest_legacy = false, then the grant is issued (never beyond the caller's current role), the decision is recorded under the policy (policy-v1: risk ceiling 4), and only on an allow the manifest is stored. A denial (403, with the decision's reason codes) or any later failure rolls the transaction back: no run, grant, decision, manifest or event remains, and no partial admitted run can be dispatched.
  3. Retries. A request that reuses an idempotency key is authorized first, then returns the original run and manifest when it is the same request from the same caller (same workflow, release selector, explicit version selector, input, files, project, release/environment/model, priority and session) even if the alias has since moved, been deactivated or now points at a version that fails a preflight, or the workflow is paused (the key is looked up, after the caller is authorized, before the target is resolved); any difference, including another caller, is a 409 (intent_conflict, one message for every difference, so it is not an oracle). "The same request" is the canonical intent: the workflow, the selectors as named (never what they resolved to), the input, the purpose and the server-derived scope. Its SHA-256 is stored in the immutable manifest as request_digest and the retry is compared with that, not with anything on the mutable run row (the intent itself is also kept in the run's summary for diagnosis; a run admitted before the digest existed is compared on its stored intent when that is complete, and is a 409 when it is not; a legacy run is compared on the fields its own row keeps). An input that is not text is compared as canonical JSON, so the key order of an object does not matter and a string that prints like the object is a different request. A trigger names its alias only if the caller did: the intent records what was asked, not the alias the trigger picked. An admitted run whose manifest is missing or cannot be read fails the retry closed (500, manifest_refused). The key's scope is (workflow, source, key), so the same key from another source or in another project's workflow is a different request. A key that names a run created while admission was off returns that legacy run (it has no manifest). Two requests racing on one key admit exactly one run, and the loser gets the same answer a later retry would (PostgreSQL scenario).
  4. Lineage (B02.4, #691). Under CALIBER_PROFILE=reference every run started through the create-run route or the event trigger names the workspace release and environment it runs against (workspace_release_id and environment_id, together; optionally model_id and config_sha256): a run without them is 422 with {"error": "lineage_required"} before anything is read or written (run_launch.require_lineage, LineageRequiredError), and the run is created with its immutable runtime lineage. A lineage that is not valid for the project (unknown or foreign release or environment, a config digest that is not the release's, a release that is not eligible) is 409; a malformed one (empty ids, a digest that is not 64 lowercase hex) is 400. A retry keeps the lineage of the run it retries (a fresh lineage record for the new run, refused with 409 if the release is no longer eligible) and a run that never had one cannot be retried in the reference profile (422). Development leaves lineage optional. Not covered, tracked: the assistant's run tool (a chat has no release to name) is refused with the same code; the cron scheduler and service-token runs, which are not admitted either, still start with no lineage (#958 and #967); and the console's Run and Trigger actions do not yet offer a release and environment, so in the reference profile they are refused until they do (#968).
  5. Who and what. The subject is the authenticated caller (session, pat or trusted_header), the workload is the workflow pinned to its version digest, the purpose is workflow_run:<path> with the route's own word (api, event, retry, assistant), never the client-chosen source field, and the scope is the fixed deployment (local organization, region and residency) plus the workflow's project. The caller must be acting in the workflow's project, and a credential bound to another project is refused (403). A workflow outside any project cannot be admitted (409, project_required); a manifest override on a manual run cannot be pinned, so it is not admitted (409, manifest_override_not_admitted).
responsecodemeaning and recovery
422lineage_requiredthe reference profile starts no run without runtime lineage: name a workspace_release_id and an environment_id together (the body is {"error": "lineage_required", ...}); nothing was stored
409project_requiredthe workflow has no project; move it into one
409bundle_unavailablecompile and publish the version again (its sealed bundle is missing, altered or unresolved)
409manifest_refuseda pin is floating or ambiguous, the rule bundle is missing or changed, or the project belongs to another organization; the message says which
409intent_conflictthe idempotency key belongs to a different request; use a new key
403source_not_approvedreference profile: a knowledge-base version the run can read (directly, through a child workflow, or on a query node) is not an approved context source of the project, or a query takes its versions from an input; approve the named versions, use the project's own knowledge bases, or name the versions on the node, then run again
409manifest_override_not_admittedsave the manifest as a version, publish it and run that
409sync_run_not_admittedsubmit the run to the queued /workflow-runs endpoint
403policy_denied / grant_refusedthe policy or the caller's role does not allow it; the reason codes are in the message
503authority_unavailablethe grant or decision store could not answer; nothing was stored, retry

Not admitted yet (stay legacy runs): runs started by the cron scheduler and by a service token (routes/services.py), because neither has a typed subject (a user who authenticated) to put in a grant; they need a service-principal model first (#958). Preview and index rows are not executable runs. Legacy runs are marked as such, never gain a manifest, and keep today's execution path.

Executing an admitted run (B02.2b, #683). The worker reads the run's manifest back (workflows/run_pins.py::load_run_manifest: digest, schema and run id checked) and executes only what it pinned. It builds the plan from the version's sealed bundle (its resolved manifest and embedded skill snapshots), so a moved deployment alias, a prompt alias pointing at new text, a skill with new content or a different active knowledge-base version changes nothing about a run that was admitted before it (scenario V10). What the bundle only names is verified against the registry before anything is built, and a mismatch fails the run closed with a named code instead of running on something else: each registered tool's definition (module, callable, backend, side-effect level, approval flag, named secrets), each MCP tool's discovered schema and policy, each child workflow (a published version whose own sealed bundle is the pinned digest, checked down the whole tree), the provider and the default model an inherit agent gets.

error codemeaning and recovery
manifest_missingan admitted run has no manifest (never produced by admission, which stores both or neither): the run is not dispatched
manifest_corruptthe stored manifest does not read back or names another run: treat as corruption of immutable evidence
pins_mismatchthe run's version, or the manifest it would execute, is not the pinned one
pins_changedthe version, a tool, an MCP tool or a child workflow is not what was pinned (recompiled, edited in place, removed, archived or unpublished): submit a new run
model_route_changedthe deployment's provider, or the default model an inherit agent would get, is not one the run was pinned to: restore it or submit a new run
authority_deniedthe run's grant, subject or workload no longer authorizes it (see "Who a run acts as"): the summary names the policy's reason codes. grant_revoked / not_a_member: submit a new run as someone who may; grant_expired: the run outlived its grant (below), submit a new run or raise CALIBER_ADMISSION_GRANT_TTL_SECONDS
authority_unavailablethe authority store could not answer: the run is failed, not dispatched (nothing is assumed allowed; a failing statement's aborted transaction is rolled back first); resubmit once it is back
grant_unbound / identity_invalidthe manifest names no grant (a run admitted by a build before B03.4, queued or parked across an upgrade, fails here: resubmit it), or its principals do not read back (corruption of immutable evidence)

Who a run acts as (B03.4, #684). After the pins check and before anything is built, the worker calls workflows/run_identity.py::identity_for_run. It takes the exact grant id the manifest names (grant_id, sealed at admission; there is no "newest grant" lookup and no ambient grant) and the subject and workload the manifest recorded, and asks the policy (decide) whether that subject, running that workload, may still resource.execute the workflow for the manifest's purpose now. It gates dispatch; it does not change which principal the run's tools act as (the MCP preflight still runs as the workflow owner). The grant must be the run's, the subject's and the workload's; not revoked or expired; the subject must still be a member of the project (or its owner) in a role that permits the action; and the policy's own checks (version, purpose, risk) must allow it. The decision is recorded, allow or deny, so a run's history shows every time it was cleared to run; nothing in the manifest, the grant or the earlier decisions is changed, and a denial revokes nothing. A resumed run is dispatched by the same worker, so a resume is checked exactly like a first run: a grant revoked or a member removed while a run waited for approval means the run fails at resume with authority_denied, having executed nothing more. A grant has a lifetime (CALIBER_ADMISSION_GRANT_TTL_SECONDS, default 24 hours from admission) and nothing renews it: a run that waits longer than that, for an approval, an event, a timer or a long queue, fails at its next dispatch with grant_expired. Size the TTL to the longest wait a workflow may have. The check's row locks (grant, membership, project) are released by a commit right after the decision, so they are not held while the plan is built. A legacy run has no identity and keeps its legacy behaviour; no grant is manufactured for it. A manifest written before it named a grant (admitted by a development build) is refused (grant_unbound) rather than guessed at.

Admission refuses a version whose child workflow has no sealed bundle to pin (409 bundle_unavailable: publish the child, then compile the parent again).

Still live at run time, said plainly: the deployment's other model settings (reasoning effort, base URL, API choice, parallel tool calls, prompt cache), MCP server addresses and credentials, the values behind named secrets, the embedding and chat models of knowledge nodes, and the contents of files and datasets that the bundle identifies by digest or version rather than embeds. A recompile of a version after a run is admitted fails that run (even one parked waiting for approval), by design.

Not done by the worker yet: checking the run's authority at each effect inside a run (it is checked once per dispatch, including resume) and fencing each transition with the execution lease.

Run principals: subject and workload#

A run acts as two distinct principals, defined as immutable values in caliber/src/caliber/policy/principal.py (B03.1, #657). The subject is who started it: user_id, auth_method (session, pat or trusted_header) and, as server-side context only, the project. The workload is what runs: a name and one workflow-version digest. The workload id is wl_ plus the full 64-hex SHA-256 digest; it is derived, never chosen, and a manifest that carries any other id is refused. Only user_id and auth_method are written for the subject: a project_id in a manifest subject is refused. The types are pure; persisting them (#680) and resolving them for a run (#684) come later, so this page lists no setting for them.

The types are stricter than the manifest schema, which accepts any non-empty string: a workload digest must be a full bare SHA-256, and an id, name or grant id may not contain control, format or line-separator characters. A user_id that caliber.auth would treat as anonymous (anonymous, any case, or one containing a comma) is refused, and so is any scope caliber.auth does not define. A pat subject becomes an identity only with its credential_id (and the token's credential_project_id when it is bound), so a project binding is never dropped.

Refusals raise PrincipalError; the recovery for each:

refusalrecovery
workload_id must be the one derived from the full workflow_version_digestbuild it with Workload.for_workflow(name, digest); never copy an id from elsewhere
workflow_version_digest must be a full lowercase 64-hex SHA-256 digestpass the workflow version's whole bare digest, not a prefix, uppercase or sha256: form; a version with no digest (a legacy version) cannot be a workload
subject must have exactly ['auth_method', 'user_id']; extra ['project_id'], missing []drop project_id from the manifest subject and pass it as Subject.from_manifest(data, project_id=...)
a pat subject needs its credential_id to become an identitypass credential_id (and credential_project_id when the token is bound) to to_identity

Run grants#

A run acts under a grant (B03.2, #664; caliber/src/caliber/policy/grants.py, migration 0115, table caliber_run_grants). It is bound to an exact run and an exact grant id, to the run's subject and workload (run principals), to a project, to explicit sets of allowed actions and resources, to the policy version it was issued under and to an expiry. Issuing one is part of admission (#680). This page lists what the store and the check guarantee:

  • Exact identifiers, no fallback. Every check names the run id and the grant id. There is no "newest grant" and no ambient one; a different run, an unknown grant and a mismatch are all grant_not_found, so ids cannot be probed.
  • Closed vocabulary, explicit sets. Actions are the names in caliber.resource_access.PROJECT_ACTIONS (an unknown action cannot be granted; release.break_glass_apply is deliberately not in it). Actions and resources match exactly: no wildcard, prefix, case folding or ordering by name or risk.
  • A grant never exceeds the subject's role. Issuing refuses an action the subject's current role is not in the set for (PROJECT_ACTIONS[action]), and every use rechecks the current role (role_not_allowed), so a demotion narrows a standing grant at once. The project owner counts as owner only when the caller supplies live scopes that still include the owner-role scopes; without them owner is treated as editor.
  • Rechecked every time, in this order: grant_revoked, grant_expired (the expiry instant itself is expired), not_a_member (the subject's current active membership, or ownership, of the grant's project), action_not_allowed (not in the grant), role_not_allowed, resource_not_allowed. A database failure while reading any of it is authority_unavailable: a denial, never an allow. Datetimes must be timezone-aware (UTC is stored).
  • Revocation and membership changes cannot be raced (PostgreSQL). A check takes a row lock on the grant and a shared lock on the membership and project rows it relied on, in the caller's transaction; a revocation, a member's removal and a demotion each wait for a check in flight, and a check that starts after one sees it. Under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE a change committed after the transaction's snapshot is authority_unavailable. Run the transition a check guards in the same transaction as the check. SQLite gives no such guarantee (the driver does not even begin a transaction before the first write); it is development only and the reference profile refuses it. SQLite's INSERT OR REPLACE also bypasses the triggers below (a development-only gap).
  • Immutable but for a whole revocation, in the database. Triggers refuse changing any column but the three revocation fields (caliber_run_grants is immutable except for revocation), refuse any change once revoked (a revoked grant stays revoked) and refuse DELETE (TRUNCATE too on PostgreSQL). A CHECK makes a revocation whole: revoked_at, revoked_by and revoke_reason are all null or all set. The ORM refuses the same (ImmutableRecordError), including editing a committed revocation. As with run manifests, run the application as a role without DELETE or TRUNCATE on the table; the profile does not check which role it uses.

Refusals and what to do:

codemeaningrecovery
grant_not_foundno grant with that exact run id and grant iduse the ids admission returned for this run; never look one up by recency
grant_revokedthe grant was revokedrequest a new run or a new grant through admission
grant_expiredexpires_at has passedthe run must be re-admitted; a grant is never extended
not_a_memberthe subject is no longer an active member (or owner) of the projectrestore the membership, or stop the run
action_not_allowedthe action is not in this grantrequest a grant that names it (it must be in the vocabulary)
role_not_allowedthe subject's current role is not allowed to perform the actionchange the role deliberately, or use a different action
resource_not_allowedthe resource is not in this grantrequest a grant that names the exact resource
authority_unavailablethe store could not answerretry after the database recovers; nothing was authorized

Issuing refuses (GrantError): an empty or oversized set, an action outside the vocabulary or beyond the subject's role, a subject who is not a current member, a run that does not exist or belongs to another project, a naive datetime, and an expiry that is not in the future.

This task stores and checks grants; it makes no policy decision and records none (B03.3 and B03.5). A rollback (caliber-migrate downgrade 0114) drops the table and therefore the grants, never the runs.

Experiment ownership#

In the reference profile CALIBER, not the first editor, decides who owns an MLflow experiment (caliber/src/caliber/observability/experiment_registry.py; B11.registry, #665; migration 0118, table caliber_experiment_owners, keyed by the tracking backend and the canonical experiment id). Registering an agent, creating or updating a workflow, or publishing from the assistant with an experiment reference:

  • creates the experiment server-side, tagged with its owner, when it does not exist (provenance=created);
  • refuses an experiment that already exists but nobody registered (409), unless an administrator is registering it, who may adopt it (provenance=adopted); and refuses a numeric id that names no experiment;
  • refuses an experiment another project or user owns (409), whichever alias (name or id) is used, even when two requests race (the primary key admits one row);
  • fails closed (503) when the tracking backend cannot answer, and registers nothing.

The authorization check (project write access) runs before the claim, so a request that is refused creates nothing. The registry row shares the request's database transaction (a rollback leaves no owner), but the MLflow experiment does not: if a request fails after CALIBER created the experiment, the experiment stays, carrying the tags CALIBER wrote (caliber.owner_kind, caliber.owner_id, caliber.created_by). The scope those tags name may register it on retry; nobody else may (an experiment without those tags is an existing one, refused as above). MLflow's own API is not scoped, so anyone who can reach it can still create or tag experiments directly.

For data from before the registry, an administrator runs POST /observability/experiment-claims/migrate once: an experiment claimed by exactly one scope becomes that scope's, one claimed by two or more is quarantined, and the report lists registered, quarantined, skipped_existing, mismatched (already registered, but a legacy claim names another scope too) and unresolved. It is safe to run again, and to run twice at once. Each quarantine is settled with POST /observability/experiment-claim-conflicts/resolve (the owner is a project that exists, a user, or public with no id; one administrator wins a race, the other gets 404). A resolved experiment is visible to its owner (under any alias it wrote, and without any text claim) and hidden from the losing scope even though that scope's old agent or workflow claim still names it; it no longer appears in the conflicts listing. The SDK has migrate_experiment_claims() and resolve_experiment_conflict(). Details of aliases, quarantine and visibility are in the observability architecture. Development keeps the earlier behaviour: an unregistered experiment goes to whoever binds it first, and a name that resolves to nothing stays a plain reference.

Known limits: the registry's key includes the tracking backend's URI (credentials and query dropped, scheme and host lower-cased, trailing slash removed), so repointing CALIBER at another server starts a new registry and a default per-directory file: store differs by working directory; use a tracking server. Fleet, prompt-target and skill-target agents that CALIBER names itself are not registered until an administrator runs the migration. There is no release or transfer path: deleting the agent or workflow does not free the experiment (an administrator cannot reassign an active owner yet).

Who may read a trace's payload (B11.4a, #672)#

Seeing that a trace exists (it is listed, counted, its metadata shown) follows the experiment's visibility. Reading what is in it (span inputs, outputs and tool arguments, which can hold personal data) is a separate, stricter permission, trace.payload.read, held by the project roles owner and editor; a reviewer or viewer is refused. caliber.observability.trace_access.can_read_payloads(session, identity, experiment) decides it:

  • the reference must name an existing experiment; its owner is the registry's active row (a quarantined row means no owner) or, for an experiment the registry has no row for (development, or before the legacy migration), the single scope all agent and workflow claims name (none, or two scopes, means no owner);
  • a project owner: the caller must be acting in that project (the active project and any project-bound credential are that project) and their current membership role must allow the action (decide_project_access(..., "trace.payload.read")); demotion, removal or deactivation take effect on the next call, and caliber.admin is not an implicit project role, so an administrator who is not a member is refused. An archived project keeps its members' access, as every other read path does;
  • a user owner: only that user. Public experiments have no payload readers (intentional: their payloads are the least accountable). No owner, a missing project, an empty or non-string reference, an unreachable tracking backend or database are all refused: the function returns False and never guesses;
  • platform scopes (caliber.viewer and so on) are not checked here; the calling route must still require them.

What a caller without it gets (B11.4b, #677). In the reference profile the trace routes decide this per experiment (once per request) before any payload goes into a response. GET /observability/traces/{id} for a caller who may see the trace but not read its payload returns the same shape with every governed field replaced by [redacted:<field>]: each span's inputs and outputs and its attributes.tool_arguments, attributes.retrieved_documents and attributes.model_output (the list is profile.GOVERNED_TRACE_FIELDS), plus the whole-trace request and response. Real tracers also put the same payload in other attributes (mlflow.spanInputs, mlflow.spanOutputs, mlflow.chat.messages, caliber.tool.input, caliber.tool.output), so redaction is fail-closed: every span attribute that is not on the short list of known payload-free ones (profile.SAFE_SPAN_ATTRIBUTES: run, node and job ids, status, model name, token and cost counts, tool name and latency, span type) is redacted as [redacted:attributes.<key>]. Keys are never deleted or added, and everything else (span ids, names, times, status, attributes.caliber.run_id, tokens, cost) is identical to what an editor sees. GET /observability/traces redacts request_preview and response_preview the same way, and GET /observability/metrics is computed from the redacted summaries (the numbers are unchanged; no payload appears). The run trace (GET /workflow-runs/{id}/trace) and the assistant's get_workflow_run_trace tool apply the same rule, decided by the run's project (owner or editor reads; a run outside any project belongs to the user who started it). A trace the caller may not see at all is still a 404, never a redacted 200. Outside the reference profile nothing is redacted, as before.

Recovery: a viewer or reviewer who needs the contents asks a project owner or editor to read them, or is made an editor (PATCH /projects/{id}/members/{user_id}); an administrator who needs them must be a member of the project (admin is not an implicit project role). Not governed, said plainly: the review-queue item view and "create example from trace" in evaluation datasets also surface trace payloads and still follow experiment visibility only (tracked in #960); a trace's tags and feedback assessments (free text that can quote a payload) are returned as before; the permission is decided after the trace has been fetched into the server's memory (it is never returned), because the experiment is only known from the trace; and MLflow's own API is unscoped (see above).

The execution-owner lease#

In the reference profile exactly one process holds the execution-owner lease and only the holder runs the background loops (ADR 0002). B13.2 (#668; caliber/src/caliber/ownership.py, migration 0116, table caliber_execution_owner) is the lease and its fencing token; the lifespan wiring that makes the loops obey it is B13.3 (#673, below). What the lease guarantees:

  • Database time. Expiry is decided by the database's clock (clock_timestamp(), so a long transaction does not see a lapsed lease as live) inside the statement that tests it; a process's own clock never extends a lease.
  • One owner. acquire returns the lease or None. It is a new acquisition only: when the lease has expired (or never existed) the token grows by exactly one (the first is 1); while a lease is held and unexpired the answer is None for everyone, including the holder's own owner_id, so a restart that reuses a stable id cannot adopt a paused predecessor's token. The holder extends its lease with renew(lease), which keeps the token.
  • Exact fencing. renew, release and assert_fenced compare the owner id and the captured token for equality, and an unexpired lease; there is no "token is older than the latest" test and no fresh read of a current token. A stale or future token, another owner's, or another lease name's, is refused (LeaseLost).
  • Fenced transitions. assert_fenced runs in the caller's transaction before an owner-only transition and, on PostgreSQL, holds a row lock until that transaction ends, so a takeover waits for the transition rather than overtaking it (the check happens under a valid lease and the transition is serialized before any takeover; the commit itself may land after the database-time expiry). SQLite gives no such guarantee; it is development only.
  • Isolation. Written for READ COMMITTED (PostgreSQL's default): a contended acquire blocks and then returns None. Under REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE a contended acquire, or a fence racing a heartbeat committed after the snapshot, raises LeaseLost (fails closed).
  • Fails closed. An unavailable lease store is LeaseLost (every database error is reported that way, programming errors included: log its __cause__), not a lease. A heartbeat that arrives after expiry extends nothing and never resurrects the lease; the process must acquire again and gets a new token.
  • Bounds (LeaseError). ttl_seconds from 1 to 3600; owner_id at most 128 characters; the lease name at most 64.

Guidance for the loop wiring: renew every ttl / 3 at most; keep fenced transactions much shorter than ttl minus the renewal interval (a fenced transaction blocks the owner's own renewal and every other fenced transition); give fenced and acquiring transactions a SET LOCAL lock_timeout, since a stuck session holding the row would block failover (idle_in_transaction_session_timeout bounds it too).

A rollback (caliber-migrate downgrade 0115) drops the table; the next acquirer starts at token 1.

Who runs the loops (B13.3, #673)#

In the reference profile the loops start only while this process holds the lease and stop when it is lost (caliber/src/caliber/execution_role.py, wired in server.py::_build_lifespan):

  • Owner or secondary. At startup a process makes one attempt to acquire, so its role is known before the first request, then ticks every CALIBER_EXECUTION_LEASE_SECONDS / 3 (default lease 30 s, minimum 3 s). The holder renews the exact lease it captured; a process that does not hold it keeps trying to acquire. /readiness carries execution_role: owner while this process runs the loops, secondary while it only serves requests (the event bus and every HTTP route run in both; no loop, webhook dispatcher, scheduler or worker runs in a secondary).
  • Losing the lease fails closed. The owner keeps a local deadline of two thirds of the lease after the start of its last successful renewal. A renewal that fails, finds the lease gone or does not answer by that deadline (a slow or hung database included) stops the loops, and the role reads secondary from the moment the stop begins; the process tries to acquire again on later ticks and a fresh acquisition has a higher token. The lease calls run on their own thread, never the loops' threads, and on PostgreSQL carry a lock_timeout and statement_timeout of a third of the lease. If the loops fail to start after an acquisition, the ones that did start are stopped, the lease is released and the process stays secondary (the error is logged and the next tick tries again).
  • Takeover. When the owner dies its lease lapses by database time and a secondary becomes the owner within one lease plus one tick plus the time to start the loops (the V14 scenario asserts 2 x the lease, SIGKILL included). A clean shutdown stops the loops while it keeps renewing the lease, then releases it, so the successor starts only after the loops have stopped and does not wait for expiry.
  • Heartbeats. caliber_worker_heartbeats therefore lists owner-only workers from one process only (the holder's).
  • Outside the reference profile there is no lease: the loops start as before when background tasks are enabled (role owner), and a process with background tasks disabled reports secondary.
  • Not yet fenced per transition. The loops still claim rows themselves, and they stop concurrently (the webhook dispatcher first). A loop mid-transition when the lease is lost finishes that transition, bounded by CALIBER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS, so an old owner's last transition can overlap a new owner's first one by up to that grace after a lease loss. Fencing each transition with assert_fenced is #684.
  • Events raised on a secondary. HTTP routes on a secondary publish webhooks and alerts (job.applied, agent.rolled_back, SLO incidents) to the in-process event bus, and no dispatcher runs there: with the default CALIBER_WORKFLOW_RUN_EVENT_BACKEND=in_process those events are not delivered by any process. Use a shared backend (database, nats or redis) so the owner's dispatcher sees them. The outbox below makes run events durable independent of the backend; it does not yet carry webhooks and alerts. Live run streams for a run that executes on the owner reach only the owner's subscribers on the in-process backend.

Events: the outbox#

A business transition and the event that announces it commit together or not at all (B13.4, #685; caliber/src/caliber/events/outbox.py). Publishing to a queue after the commit loses the event when the process dies between the two; publishing before it announces something that never happened. So there is no queue in the transaction: append_run_event writes the run event and a caliber_event_outbox row inside one savepoint, and a background publisher delivers the rows afterwards.

  • On in the reference profile, or anywhere with CALIBER_EVENT_OUTBOX_ENABLED=true. Off, nothing changes.
  • The row is the event. event_id is run-event:<run id>:<sequence>, so recording it twice is the same row; the same id with different content is refused (OutboxConflict). The row holds an ADR 0003 event_envelope (the payload is referenced by dataref and datahash, never inlined) and the payload itself.
  • Delivery is at least once. OutboxPublisher (an owner-only loop; it appears in the worker inventory) claims due rows one by one with a conditional update (exclusive on SQLite too; FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on PostgreSQL) and a lease, hands each to every registered consumer (one that is down does not keep the others from the event), and marks the row delivered. A consumer that fails is retried with exponential backoff (CALIBER_EVENT_OUTBOX_MAX_ATTEMPTS, default 20); a row that exhausts its attempts is dead and kept for an operator. The attempt is counted when the row is claimed, so an event whose handoff kills the process or hangs still runs out of attempts. A publisher that dies holding a claim is covered by the lease: the row is due again when it expires, and a second publisher redelivers it; a publisher that outlives its lease can no longer settle the row. Lease times come from the publishers' clocks (one publisher runs at a time, the execution owner).
  • Stopping. Losing the lease or shutting down finishes the handoff in flight (bounded by CALIBER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS), releases the rest of the batch without counting an attempt, and claims nothing more.
  • No payload in errors. last_error and the log carry the consumer's name and the exception class, never its message (a database error's text can include the statement's parameters, which are the payload).
  • Consumers deduplicate. SqlInboxConsumer acknowledges by committing a row in caliber_event_inbox whose key is (consumer, event_id), so a redelivery after a crash is ignored; claim_unprocessed (a plain read: no lock, no lease) and mark_processed (idempotent) let a single consumer track its own work.
  • A full notification queue loses nothing. The in-process bus and SSE stay notifications: a slow subscriber's bounded queue drops its copy. The outbox row was committed with the transition and is delivered regardless.
  • Retention. Delivered rows are pruned after CALIBER_EVENT_OUTBOX_RETENTION_DAYS (default 7); dead rows are kept, and so are inbox rows (a consumer's own retention). Deleting a workflow deletes its runs' outbox and inbox rows with them.
  • What it does not do yet. The default registers no consumer, so rows are delivered at once and pruned; it publishes nothing to the bus or to webhooks (that would duplicate the notifications that exist). Webhook and alert events are not in the outbox. Consumers arrive with the features that need them.

Inbound events: the inbox#

An inbound event (a webhook, a connector callback) can be sent twice, arrive on two workers at once, or reach a process that dies half way through. caliber/src/caliber/events/inbox.py (B13.5a, #689) makes each one apply once. This is the inbox for events from outside; caliber_event_inbox above is the end of our own outbox handoff and is unchanged.

  • Identity is (consumer, source, event_id), the primary key of caliber_inbox_events. The row also stores the payload_hash (sha256:<hex>, from caliber.events.outbox.payload_hash) the event arrived with and a status: received, processed or ignored.
  • One transaction. process_once(session, consumer=..., source=..., event_id=..., payload_hash=..., apply=...) inserts the reservation, runs apply (the business transition, in your session), and marks the row processed, inside savepoints of your transaction. It never commits: you commit, so the three stand or fall together. Handing the event to a durable queue instead is the same call with an apply that calls caliber.events.outbox.enqueue; the sender may be answered once that commit returns.
  • Results. processed (with apply's value), duplicate (the same identity and payload were already taken: acknowledge it, nothing is applied) or ignored (apply raised InboxIgnored: whatever it wrote is undone and the row is recorded, so a redelivery is a duplicate).
  • Refusals. The same identity with a different payload raises InboxPayloadMismatch (a different message reusing an id; the stored hash is never overwritten and nothing is applied). A blank, over-long or control-character-bearing consumer (64), source (64) or event_id (160), or a payload_hash that is not sha256: plus 64 lowercase hex digits, raises ValueError before the database is touched.
  • Recovery. If apply raises, the reservation goes with it, so the sender's retry is processed: a failed transaction is never treated as already processed. If the process dies before the commit, the database discards the transaction and the outcome is the same. Concurrent duplicates serialise on the primary key: on PostgreSQL the second waits for the first (with no timeout of its own: a first delivery that hangs holds the key, so give the transaction a lock_timeout), then reports duplicate if it committed or takes over if it rolled back. On SQLite a concurrent duplicate fails at once with a lock error and the retry is a duplicate.
from caliber.events.inbox import process_once
from caliber.events.outbox import payload_hash

with session_factory() as session:
    result = process_once(
        session,
        consumer="documents",
        source="connector",
        event_id=delivery_id,
        payload_hash=payload_hash(body),
        apply=lambda: advance_run(session, body),
    )
    session.commit()
# result.outcome is "processed", "duplicate" or "ignored"; InboxPayloadMismatch means answer 409
  • Limits. This is at-most-once application per key, not exactly-once delivery: the sender may still send it many times, and each is acknowledged. apply must not commit or roll back the session (if it does, InboxContractError is raised; its writes may already be committed with a reservation still received, which every later delivery sees as a duplicate and an operator must resolve), and a side effect outside the transaction (a call to another service) is not covered by it. Rows are kept until prune(session, older_than=...) forgets them; use a cutoff older than the sender's longest redelivery window, because a forgotten id is applied again. Nothing calls process_once yet: wiring the GitHub webhook and the connector callback is B13.5b (#693).

Effect proposals#

A run that asks to change something outside CALIBER first records a proposal (B05.1, #700, ADR 0003; caliber/src/caliber/effects/records.py, table caliber_effect_proposals, migration 0123). Nothing writes one yet: the dispatcher that does arrives with the rest of B05 (#705 onwards). What exists is the record and the rules it keeps.

  • Two separate things. The logical key (deployment, run, node, occurrence_id) says which effect: a retry presents the same occurrence and finds the same proposal, a legitimate repeat (a loop that notifies the same endpoint twice) presents the next occurrence and gets its own. The intent says what exactly: Intent(connector, connector_version, effect_class, resource, args, expected_resource_version), stored as canonical JSON (intent_bytes) with its algorithm (intent-v1) and its digest intent_hash (sha256: plus 64 hex digits; on PostgreSQL a CHECK ties the digest to the bytes). Changing the connector version, the effect class or any other intent field changes the digest.
  • One digest, reused. Approvals and receipts compare against Intent.digest (equivalently the stored intent_hash) and never compute a hash over fewer fields, so an approval of one intent cannot cover another.
  • Same key, same intent: idempotent. Same key, different intent: refused. record_proposal returns the existing proposal (created=False) for a retry and raises ProposalConflict (code intent_conflict; the calling route answers 409) for a different intent; the stored intent stands and the error carries the key and both digests, never the arguments. A malformed field (blank, over-long or control-character-bearing text, non-JSON arguments, an unknown effect class, an intent over 256 KiB) raises ProposalError with code bad_field; an unknown run, run_not_found; a constraint failure that is not the key, store_failed (without the driver's text, which would carry the arguments). args must be plain JSON of exact Python types (string-keyed dict, list, str, int, finite float, bool, None, nested at most 64 deep) so two different Python values never share a digest; the converse is not promised (intent-v1 is not RFC 8785): 1 and 1.0, or NFC and NFD spellings, are different intents, and a retry that respells one gets a conflict, never a silent match.
  • Immutable. Database triggers refuse a change to any column but state, refuse DELETE (and TRUNCATE on PostgreSQL), and the ORM refuses the same. On SQLite (development) raw SQL can still bypass them with INSERT OR REPLACE or by deleting a run with foreign keys off; PostgreSQL has no such path. state is recorded as proposed; its transition rules are B05.2 (#705). A workflow whose runs have proposals cannot be deleted (409, "immutable effect proposals"), and retention never prunes such a run.
  • Reading is checked. read_proposal rebuilds the ADR 0003 proposal v1 record (with the optional occurrence_id, connector_version and intent_algorithm) and recomputes the intent from the stored columns: an edited row is corrupt, and an intent algorithm this build does not know is unsupported_algorithm, never read as the nearest.
from caliber.effects.records import Intent, ProposalConflict, record_proposal

intent = Intent(
    connector="document-request",
    connector_version="1.0.0",
    effect_class="irreversible_write",
    resource="cases/MORT-1/document-requests",
    args={"document_type": "pay_statement"},
    expected_resource_version="7",
)
with session_factory() as session:
    try:
        recorded = record_proposal(
            session, workflow_run_id=run_id, node_id="ask", occurrence_id=occurrence_id, intent=intent
        )
        session.commit()  # recorded.created is False when this effect was already recorded
    except ProposalConflict as conflict:
        session.rollback()  # answer 409: conflict.stored_intent_hash is the one on record
  • Limits. The occurrence id is allocated and persisted by the caller before the effect is attempted; this module records it and cannot tell whether a caller reused one wrongly. deployment is this installation's one configured organization (ADR 0001). Receipts, the transition table and the dispatcher are not here (B05.2 to B05.5).

Approved context sources#

A run's context may only come from sources its project has approved (B07, #692). The inventory is caliber_approved_context_sources (caliber/src/caliber/context/sources.py): one row per (project, knowledge base, version), unique. approve_source(session, project_id, knowledge_base_id, version_id, actor) records an approval, revoke_source(...) withdraws it (the row stays, with revoked_at and revoked_by, as evidence) and is_approved(session, project_id, knowledge_base_id, version_id) answers whether it is approved now (False once revoked, for anything never approved and for a source that no longer exists). Admission reads it (B07.1b, #696): under CALIBER_PROFILE=reference every knowledge-base version a run can read must be approved for the run's project (require_approved, called by prepare_admission, so create-run, trigger, retry and the assistant tool all pass through it). That is the versions in the sealed bundle's dependency lock, the versions named on a knowledge-query node that names only version_ids, and the versions read by every child workflow the run calls (each child's own sealed bundle, which must be the one the parent was compiled against). A query whose version_ids arrive on an input port cannot be pinned, so it is refused outright. Otherwise the run is refused with 403, reason_code: source_not_approved in the error body and every unapproved knowledge_base_id@version_id named in the message, and nothing is stored. The role check (resource.execute on the project) comes first, so only a caller who may run the workflow learns what the project has approved. Approval and revocation take effect at the next admission: an idempotent retry of a request that was already admitted still returns that run, and a run already admitted keeps running on what it was pinned to (the load-time check is B07.2, #699). Not covered: cron-scheduler and service-token runs, which are not admitted in the first place (#958). A knowledge base that belongs to another project or to no project can never be approved for this one (only a project's own knowledge bases can), so a workflow pinned to one is refused until it uses one of the project's own. Development does not require approval. The refusal is not audited (it carries no policy decision); the response is the record.

  • A version, not a knowledge base. Approving version 1 approves nothing else; a new build must be approved on its own.
  • Only a project's own, real sources. The knowledge base must belong to the project and the version to that knowledge base. Every miss (unknown id, another project's knowledge base, a version of a different knowledge base) is one source_not_found refusal whose message names no identifier, so a foreign id cannot be probed.
  • Idempotent and race-safe. Approving an approved source returns the existing row; concurrent approvals create one (the unique key decides). Approving a revoked source reactivates the row with the new approver and time. Revoking a source that is not approved is not_approved. The row is read from the database and locked (FOR UPDATE on PostgreSQL) before it changes, so concurrent revocations or reactivations change and audit it once, and never overwrite who revoked it.
  • Completed builds of live knowledge bases only. The version must be completed (the rule that gates activating a version) and the knowledge base not archived; otherwise it is source_not_found. An approval whose version or knowledge base has since been deleted no longer counts (is_approved is false and approved_sources omits it); the row stays as evidence.
  • Audited. Approval and revocation each write an audit row (approve_context_source / revoke_context_source, entity context_source, ids only). The functions do not commit; they do not decide who may approve (the caller's project-role check does).
  • Not a foreign key to the knowledge base. The inventory outlives a deleted knowledge base on purpose; the loader must still check the version exists.

Authorizing a source before it is loaded (B07.2, #699)#

In the reference profile the run's own grant lists the context sources it may read: admission adds the action context.read and one resource per source, knowledge_base:<knowledge_base_id>@<version_id>, for exactly the sources it approved (the bundle's, its query nodes' and its child workflows'). When the worker builds an admitted run's plan it hands the knowledge-query runner a guard (caliber.context.authorize.source_guard_for), and the runner calls it with each version it is about to query, before the retrieval service is touched. The guard runs authorize_source(session, identity, run_manifest, grant_id, knowledge_base_id, version_id):

  1. the run's subject (derived from its stored manifest by identity_for_run) must equal the subject the manifest being checked recorded (identity_mismatch; a guard against mixing manifests, not a second authentication);
  2. the source must still be approved for the project (source_not_approved; a withdrawal after admission lands here and writes an audit row context_read_denied with ids only; no policy question is asked for a withdrawn source);
  3. decide(...) is asked with the manifest's run id, the exact grant id the manifest names, the manifest's typed subject and workload, context.read, the exact source resource and the manifest's purpose: a grant that does not list the source is resource_not_allowed, another run's grant grant_not_found, a member who left not_a_member, a revoked or expired grant is refused, and the decision (allow or deny) is recorded and audited like any other.

Every refusal is a ContextDenied with one fixed message that names no source (<code> (<reasons>): this run may not read that context source); the node fails and the run fails with the stable run error code context_denied (the code and the policy's reasons are in the summary), and nothing was loaded. An authority store that cannot answer is a refusal (authority_unavailable), and a database message is never put in the node's error text. context.read is a project action (owner, editor, reviewer) with policy risk 2. The guard is passed to child workflows the run calls.

run errormeaning and recovery
context_denied with source_not_approvedthe source was approved at admission and withdrawn since: approve it again, or resubmit the run on an approved version
context_denied with authority_denied (not_a_member) / grant_revoked / grant_expiredthe run's subject left the project, or its grant was revoked or ran out: resubmit as someone who may
context_denied with authority_denied (action_not_allowed) or (resource_not_allowed)the run's grant does not list that source (a run admitted before sources were authorized, or a query that reads a version the run was not admitted for): resubmit the run
context_denied with authority_unavailablethe authority store could not answer: nothing was loaded; resubmit when it is back

What it does not do. The guard follows how the run was admitted: it is built when the run's grant carries context.read (or this deployment requires approved sources), so a run admitted with sources stays guarded under any worker configuration. A run admitted before sources were authorized has no context.read and fails where sources are required (resubmit it). A grant holds at most 256 resources, so a run with 256 or more sources is refused at admission (grant_refused). The check is point-in-time: a withdrawal landing between the guard and the query does not stop that one read. Outputs a run already produced (replayed on a resume from a checkpoint) are not re-authorized. Each version queried costs one decision and one audit row (a query naming several versions authorizes each before any is read). Legacy runs have no guard. Not covered, tracked in #973: preview runs, evaluations, deploy gates, refinement and calibration, the assistant's knowledge tools, runtime export and knowledge_build nodes still read knowledge-base bytes without this check, and cron and service-token runs are not admitted (#958).

The context manifest#

What an agent step is given is recorded before the provider sees it (B07.3a, #704): caliber.context.manifest builds a context_manifest v1 record (ADR 0003) and stores it once in caliber_context_manifests, as canonical JSON with its SHA-256 (the record has no digest field: the digest excludes itself), unique per (run, step request, revision). Re-assembling a step is a new revision, never an edit; a revision that skips ahead or repeats is refused. UPDATE and DELETE are refused by database triggers and by the ORM (and, as for run manifests, run the application as a role without those privileges).

A manifest lists the segments in the order the provider sees them (position equals the index), each with (a segment's kind must match its source: a knowledge base's text can only be retrieved_text, an instruction can only come from a prompt):

  • a trust tier: instruction only for a system or workflow instruction (and every one is); everything else, the user's input, retrieved text, tool output, history and memory, is data. Text a source contains can never be promoted to an instruction by being retrieved;
  • its source (prompt, input, knowledge-base version, tool, memory, history), the retrieval and transform that produced it, and the digest of its content (the content is not stored in the manifest);
  • for payload loaded from a knowledge base or memory, the authorization decision id of the recorded context.read allow that let it be loaded: a segment without one is refused (unauthorized_payload), and storing the manifest checks each id against the recorded decision (an allow, of that action, for this run, of that exact source: knowledge_base:<kb>@<version> or memory:<reference>, decided no later than the manifest). A decision authorizes a read, not a step, so any step of its run may cite it;
  • the omitted and redacted items and the token allocation (budget, used, instruction, data; used is the sum of the segments and may not exceed the budget).

Storing also checks that the run exists and that the record's scope and project are the deployment's and the run's, and stores only canonical bytes. content_digest is a plain SHA-256 of the content, so a short, guessable value (a yes/no, an id) can be confirmed offline by anyone who can read the manifest: treat the record as evidence for the project's members and platform administrators, and do not expose it more widely without a keyed digest.

Reading a manifest back (read_context_manifest) re-checks the digest, the schema (an unknown schema_version is unknown_version, never read as the nearest) and every rule above, so a reordered or relabelled record is caught twice, by its digest and by its positions. Refusals carry a stable code: invalid_manifest, unknown_version, tier_violation, unauthorized_payload, ordering, tokens, authorization_rejected, duplicate_revision, revision_gap. Nothing here talks to a provider.

Recorded for every agent step (B07.3b, #710). For an admitted run in the reference profile the worker hands the runtime a recorder (caliber.context.assembly.context_recorder_for, built together with the source guard), and the runtime calls it with each agent step's initial context (the step's instructions as resolved when it is assembled, its skills, its history and the one input the provider is sent, with the node whose edge delivered it) before any of it reaches the provider, for every agent, every handoff target (a native Agents SDK handoff runs inside the provider call, so every agent the step may reach is recorded first) and in child workflows too. The recorder labels the assembly: the agent's own instructions are the only instruction tier; the history is one history data segment; text a knowledge query delivered straight to the agent is retrieved_text (one segment per version it read, citing the context.read decision the guard recorded when it authorized that version); the run's own input is user_input; any other text is tool_output of the node that delivered it, or of unknown origin (an item a for_each, loop or error_boundary hands an inline agent, text a knowledge query's output reached only through another node), which is still data and is never labelled the run's own input. It builds, validates and stores the manifest (its own short transaction, committed) as revision 1 of a fresh step request. If it cannot (an unknown or unauthorized source, a refused manifest, a database failure) the step does not run: the node fails (a for_each item or an error_boundary does not absorb the refusal), the run ends context_denied and the provider was never called. A document that says "ignore all previous instructions" is therefore recorded as data and reaches the agent as input, never as part of its instructions (scenario V03).

Caps and redaction (B07.4, #719). caliber.context.manifest.pack_context(segments, caps=..., redactor=...) is the one pure function that decides what an agent step's context may contain, and build_context_manifest records its result (omitted, redacted and sections=). It redacts every data-tier segment with the PII redactor (the same one the audit log uses, CALIBER_PII_REDACTION_*; an instruction is the operator's own text and is never altered) before the digest is taken, so the manifest hashes what the provider is given and the matched text is never recorded: a changed segment gets one redacted entry (fields: ["content"], reason: "redactor:pattern-1,pattern-3", naming which rules fired); a segment that is nothing but the replacement marker is dropped and listed in omitted as redacted. It caps the retrieved and history sections at CALIBER_CONTEXT_SECTION_CAPS (JSON, default {"retrieved": 4000, "history": 2000}; only those two names are accepted and each cap is a positive integer, else the service refuses to start; a section left out is uncapped): chunks are kept in order while they fit, and the first chunk that does not fit and every later one in that section (they rank below it) is dropped and listed in omitted with reason token_budget and its tokens. The manifest's token_allocation.sections records each capped section's cap_tokens and used_tokens, and the manifest refuses a record where they do not add up to its segments. Example: with a cap of 10 and three retrieved chunks of 8 tokens, the manifest keeps the first chunk and lists two as token_budget; a chunk containing alice@example.com is hashed and recorded as ... [REDACTED] .... Not yet applied to a live step: the agent-step adapters (B08) call pack_context to decide what the provider receives. The recorder above (B07.3b) records the context as the runtime passes it and does not pack it, so until B08 consumes it no provider input is capped or redacted and the manifests it writes carry no sections; a manifest never claims a cap or a redaction that was not applied. The issue's draft names (allocation, redactions, budget) map onto the shipped v1 record (token_allocation.sections, redacted, token_budget), which is kept so manifests already written stay valid.
