What this does not cover, so it is not claimed: the tool specifications, the structured-output suffix and the results of tool calls made during a step are not in the manifest; a registry prompt is loaded when the step is assembled and again by the provider adapter, so an alias moved in between is not detected; session memory loaded for the step is recorded as history without a memory authorization (follow-up); a resumed run that replays a recorded knowledge-query output has no guard decision for it and is refused; a manifest is not linked to the NodeStep it describes, so a retried step adds a further revision-1 manifest; other model calls (a knowledge query's own answer synthesis, guardrail judges) are not agent steps and are not recorded. Token counts are an accounting estimate (four characters a token, and the recorded budget is the larger of the configured one and the total); enforcing a budget on a provider call is B08. Legacy runs and development have no recorder.

Policy decisions#

caliber.policy.decisions.decide(...) (B03.3, #671; migration 0117, table caliber_policy_decisions) answers "may this run do this action on this resource, for this purpose, right now?" with a typed PolicyDecision and records it, allow or deny, immutably (ADR 0003 policy_decision v1 plus the run, subject and workload it was asked about; there are no foreign keys, so a decision about a grant that does not exist is still evidence).

  • Exact identity, no fallback. The caller supplies run_id, grant_id, the Subject and the Workload. A different run, an unknown grant, another subject (user, authentication method or project) and another workload each deny, and nothing is looked up by recency.
  • One reason, a fixed order: grant_not_found, subject_mismatch, workload_mismatch, grant_revoked, grant_expired, not_a_member, action_not_allowed, role_not_allowed, resource_not_allowed (the run grant checks, including the current membership and role), then the policy's own: policy_version_mismatch (the grant was issued under another policy version), purpose_not_allowed, explicit_deny, unknown_action_risk and risk_above_ceiling. An unavailable store is authority_unavailable. An allow carries no reason codes.
  • Explicit maps, never ordering. Each action has an explicit risk number in the policy (every action in resource_access.PROJECT_ACTIONS must have one; a test fails otherwise), compared with the policy's ceiling. policy-v1 has a ceiling of 4 (risk equal to the ceiling is allowed). Risk 5 means "a person, never a run": project administration (archive, restore, members, ownership transfer) and every approval or acceptance (resource.approve, release.approve, release.quality_signoff, change_request.accept), so no grant can make a run approve its own work (Beta keeps a human accountable owner and human protected-action approval, ADR 0004). Explicit denies are exact (action, resource) pairs. A Policy is read-only and type-checked.
  • Replayable. input_hash is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of every input (run, grant, subject, workload, action, resource, purpose and the live scopes) plus the policy's own digest; the clock is not an input. The same inputs under the same policy hash identically.
  • Transactions. A decision is flushed, never committed. For initial admission the run, its grant and the decision share one uncommitted transaction and the caller commits only after an allow; a denial rolls all of it back. If an decision cannot be recorded, the answer is a deny with persisted = False (an allow becomes authority_unavailable; a deny keeps its reason and gains authority_unavailable), and PolicyDecision.allowed is true only for a recorded allow. A decision never touches the run manifest. The record is written in a savepoint, so a failed record never poisons the caller's transaction. Consumers must know: a denied initial admission rolls its decision row back with the transaction, so evidence of a denial must be written separately (the audit record of B03.5, or a decision made in its own transaction), and on SQLite (development only) a savepoint that is the first write of a transaction commits it, so call decide after the run and grant writes.
  • Callers must not leak identity mismatches. decide records the specific reason (subject_mismatch and workload_mismatch reveal that a grant exists). It is server-internal: any layer that answers a client (HTTP, the admission API) must collapse identity and grant-lookup failures into one uniform refusal. purpose is stored verbatim: it names why, never context or payload.
  • Malformed input is a bug, not a decision. A blank, oversized or control-character id, action, resource or purpose, a naive now, or a non-Subject raises DecisionInputError and records nothing.
  • Immutable. Triggers refuse UPDATE and DELETE (TRUNCATE too on PostgreSQL) and the ORM raises ImmutableRecordError; as with run manifests, run the application as a role without those privileges.
  • Audited (B03.5, #688). Every recorded decision also writes one audit-log row through audit.record, in the decision's own savepoint, so the two exist together: action is policy_allow (severity standard) or policy_deny (severity high, or standard when every reason is ordinary lifecycle: grant_expired, grant_revoked, not_a_member), actor the subject, entity_type policy_decision, entity_id the decision id, and details the run, grant and workload ids, the action, resource and purpose, the result, the reason codes, the policy version and the input hash. The run's input, context and any secret are never in it (and the audit log's redactor runs over it anyway). If the decision and its audit row cannot be written (the store is down) the answer is an unrecorded deny (authority_unavailable) and one structured error log line carries the decision, run, grant, action and result; nothing is allowed that is not on record. At initial admission the decision's own rows are rolled back with the refused run (nothing about a refused run is stored), so the denial's audit row is written afterwards in its own short transaction from the decision's ids and reasons (admission.record_denial; a failure there is logged and never changes the refusal).

Recovery: grant_*, not_a_member, role_not_allowed, action_not_allowed and resource_not_allowed are as in the grant table above; policy_version_mismatch means the run must be admitted again under the current policy; purpose_not_allowed and explicit_deny are policy decisions to change deliberately, not retry; risk_above_ceiling means the action cannot be done by a run (use the human-approval path or a person); unknown_action_risk means the policy lacks a risk for the action and must be extended; subject_mismatch and workload_mismatch are always a bug or an attack: fix the caller.

Not enforced yet#

ADR 0001 describes the whole reference shape; this table is what the process checks today. Not checked:

  • The shape itself: one tenant and region, MLflow addressed by MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI, an S3-compatible object store, at least two projects, and one real model provider next to the scripted adapter. Readiness reporting for MLflow and the object store is #535. The PostgreSQL version and the pgvector extension are checked by the migrations (migration 0060) and the migration-parity CI job, not by the profile.
  • Origin rules (#533). ADR 0001 names them, but #533 has no allowed-origins task yet; that rule is not scheduled.
  • The trusted-connector set (#534), refusing code-execution paths and the full attack pack (#535), a single execution owner (#536) and the Apply separation-of-duties flag (#589).
  • Cookie flags: auth_session_cookie_secure is not checked.
  • The database role: whether the application connects as a role without UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE on caliber_run_manifests (see "Run manifests are written once").

A configuration that passes this page is the minimum for the reference profile, not the whole of it.
